title: I asked for inconsistent pixel art on purpose
author: Ok-Line2658
selftext:
This frame is a deliberately bad baseline, not an accidental before shot. I asked Makeplay for one fixed night market scene with a courier bicycle, six stalls, three customers, lanterns, wet pavement, signs, crates, and steam. The prompt also asked it to mix pixel detail levels and outline weights.

The result gave me several different kinds of mismatch at once. Some stall signs are blank light rectangles while others are dense and hard to read. The customer sprites disagree on scale and silhouette. Steam, reflections, crates, lanterns, and the title all compete in the same frame.

What I cannot tell from the frame alone is which variation should survive a cleanup. The thick outline on one stall may be useful hierarchy rather than noise. The smaller customer may need more contrast rather than more pixels.

There is no after image yet. For now this is only a map of decisions that an actual art pass would have to make.

I wanted to see what a very small game brief would do, so I wrote one sentence. Guide a paper boat through floating gates before the timer runs out.

Makeplay turned that into a working browser game with 12 gates, a 42 second clock, several control options, current bands, scoring, bonuses, generated art, and sound. Most of those choices were reasonable. None of them had been requested.

The useful lesson was not that the tool added too much. My sentence described a destination but contained no boundaries. I had left the number of gates, control scheme, failure rule, visual scope, and feedback system open, then mentally treated them as settled.

My no code checklist now has two columns. The first says what must happen. The second says what must not be invented. That second column has been doing more work.
